prompt: To determine whether the tire's volume influences the tire pressure, the experimenters should most likely:

choices.text: Vary both the tire's volume and the air temperature at the same time in each trial, measuring the tire pressure
choices.rationale: Changing two factors at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any change.

choices.text: Measure the tire's volume in each trial of Experiment 1 instead of measuring the tire pressure
choices.rationale: Measuring the tire's volume does not test its effect; it must be deliberately varied.

choices.text: Vary the tire's volume while holding the air temperature and all other conditions constant
choices.rationale: Correct. To test a new factor, change only that factor and hold everything else, including the original independent variable, constant.

choices.text: Repeat Experiment 1 exactly as before, but with a larger number of values of the air temperature
choices.rationale: This gives more detail about temperature but never changes the tire's volume.

explanation: A fair test of the tire's volume changes it alone. The air temperature, which was the variable in Experiment 1, must now be held fixed.

table.caption: Experiment 1: A sealed bicycle tire was placed in a chamber whose temperature could be set. At each temperature the tire was left for 30 minutes and its pressure was then read with a gauge. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: A student claims that the cricket species affects the chirping rate. Do the results of Experiments 1 and 2 support this claim?

choices.text: No; the two experiments gave the same chirp rate at every temperature tested
choices.rationale: The columns differ at every temperature; compare them row by row.

choices.text: No; the chirping rate increased as temperature increased in both experiments
choices.rationale: A shared trend with temperature says nothing about whether the cricket species matters; the two columns differ at every row.

choices.text: Yes; the chirping rate increased as temperature increased in both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2
choices.rationale: That trend concerns temperature, not the cricket species; it would appear even if the condition had no effect.

choices.text: Yes; at every temperature tested, the chirping rate was higher for Species B than for Species A
choices.rationale: Correct. The two experiments differ only in this condition, and the results differ consistently between them.

explanation: Because the experiments differ only in the cricket species, the consistent gap between the two sets of results (higher for Species B) shows that the condition affects the chirping rate.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students kept a cricket in a ventilated container inside a chamber using a cricket of Species A whose temperature could be set. After the cricket had been at each temperature for 20 minutes, they counted its chirps for one minute. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using a cricket of Species B, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which experiment(s) provide the information needed to determine whether the temperature of the tubes affects the activity of the enzyme?

choices.text: Neither experiment, because the pH of the solution was varied in both of them
choices.rationale: Varying pH in both experiments is what makes them comparable row by row; the comparison across experiments is exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Experiment 2 alone, because it was the only experiment performed and kept the tubes at 35°C
choices.rationale: Experiment 2 also used only one setting of the temperature of the tubes; a comparison is required.

choices.text: Experiments 1 and 2 together, because they differ only in the temperature of the tubes
choices.rationale: Correct. Only by comparing results obtained under the two conditions, with everything else the same, can the effect of that condition be isolated.

choices.text: Experiment 1 alone, because it tested the full range of the pH of the solution under one condition
choices.rationale: Experiment 1 used a single setting of the temperature of the tubes, so by itself it cannot reveal its effect.

explanation: Each experiment holds the temperature of the tubes fixed at one setting; the two settings differ between experiments, so comparing Experiments 1 and 2 isolates its effect.

stimulus.title: Enzyme Activity and pH
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students added 1 mL of enzyme solution to tubes containing a substrate solution buffered to a set pH and kept the tubes at 25°C. They measured how much product formed in 5 minutes to find the activity. Each pH was tested in triplicate.
Results (the activity of the enzyme): at pH 5, 32 µmol/min; at pH 6, 57 µmol/min; at pH 7, 49 µmol/min; at pH 8, 20 µmol/min; at pH 9, 4 µmol/min.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated and kept the tubes at 35°C, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at pH 5, 47 µmol/min; at pH 6, 84 µmol/min; at pH 7, 73 µmol/min; at pH 8, 30 µmol/min; at pH 9, 6 µmol/min.

prompt: If a third experiment used an incubation temperature of 34°C and all other conditions of Experiments 1 and 2, the number of colonies at 10 µg/mL would most likely be:

choices.text: below both experiments' results, less than 72 colonies
choices.rationale: This is below both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: between 31 colonies and 43 colonies
choices.rationale: These are the results for 15 µg/mL, not 10 µg/mL.

choices.text: above both experiments' results, greater than 99 colonies
choices.rationale: This is above both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: between 72 colonies and 99 colonies
choices.rationale: Correct. At 10 µg/mL, Experiment 1 gave 72 and Experiment 2 gave 99; an intermediate setting should give an intermediate result.

explanation: The two experiments bracket the new setting, so the result at 10 µg/mL should lie between 72 and 99 colonies.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students spread 0.1 mL of a bacterial culture onto agar plates containing a known concentration of an antibiotic and incubated the plates at 30°C. After 24 hours they counted the colonies on each plate. Three plates were prepared for each concentration and the average count was recorded. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated and incubated the plates at 37°C, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: The design of Experiment 1 has a weakness. Which statement best describes it?

choices.text: Only a single value of the temperature of the water was tested, so no trend could possibly be identified
choices.rationale: The results list 6 different values of water temperature.

choices.text: The temperature of the water was deliberately changed from trial to trial instead of being held constant throughout
choices.rationale: Changing the independent variable is the point of the experiment, not a flaw.

choices.text: The volume of water changed between trials, confounding the effect of the temperature of the water
choices.rationale: Correct. A second factor that changes along with the independent variable confounds the results.

choices.text: The dissolved oxygen concentration was measured in every trial rather than only in the final trial of the series
choices.rationale: The dependent variable must be measured in every trial.

explanation: Good design changes only water temperature. Because the volume of water also changed, any difference in dissolved oxygen could be due to either factor.

stimulus.title: Water Temperature and Dissolved Oxygen
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students bubbled air through a beaker of water held at a set temperature until no more oxygen would dissolve, then measured the dissolved oxygen with an oxygen probe. Because of limited equipment, the volume of water was different for each trial.
Results (the dissolved oxygen concentration): at 5 °C, 12.6 mg/L; at 10 °C, 11.2 mg/L; at 15 °C, 10.1 mg/L; at 20 °C, 9.3 mg/L; at 25 °C, 8.8 mg/L; at 30 °C, 8.6 mg/L.

prompt: Which of the following conclusions is NOT supported by the results of Experiment 1?

choices.text: The dissolved oxygen concentration was greater at 5 °C than at 15 °C.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The salt content of the water does not affect the dissolved oxygen concentration.
choices.rationale: Correct. The salt content of the water was not varied in Experiment 1, so nothing can be concluded about it.

choices.text: The dissolved oxygen concentration was greater at 5 °C than at 30 °C.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The dissolved oxygen concentration was greater at 20 °C than at 25 °C.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

explanation: Three of the statements can be checked against the table and hold. "The salt content of the water does not affect the dissolved oxygen concentration." cannot: the salt content of the water was not varied in Experiment 1, so nothing can be concluded about it.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students bubbled air through a beaker of water held at a set temperature until no more oxygen would dissolve, then measured the dissolved oxygen with an oxygen probe. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: Suppose the experimenters wanted to test whether the compression of the spring affects the horizontal distance the ball traveled. Which change to the procedure of Experiment 1 would best test this?

choices.text: Measure the compression of the spring in each trial of Experiment 1 instead of measuring the horizontal distance the ball traveled
choices.rationale: Measuring the compression of the spring does not test its effect; it must be deliberately varied.

choices.text: Vary the compression of the spring while holding the launch angle and all other conditions constant
choices.rationale: Correct. To test a new factor, change only that factor and hold everything else, including the original independent variable, constant.

choices.text: Vary both the compression of the spring and the launch angle at the same time in each trial, measuring the horizontal distance the ball traveled
choices.rationale: Changing two factors at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused any change.

choices.text: Repeat Experiment 1 exactly as before, but with a larger number of values of the launch angle
choices.rationale: This gives more detail about launch angle but never changes the compression of the spring.

explanation: A fair test of the compression of the spring changes it alone. The launch angle, which was the variable in Experiment 1, must now be held fixed.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students used a spring launcher to fire the same ball at a set angle above the horizontal, always with the spring compressed by the same amount. They measured the horizontal distance from the launcher to the landing point. Each angle was fired three times and the average distance recorded. Table 1 lists the results.

prompt: A student claims that the mass of the bob affects the period of the pendulum. Do the results of Experiments 1 and 2 support this claim?

choices.text: No; at every string length tested, the two experiments gave the same period
choices.rationale: Correct. Changing the condition left every result unchanged, so the results give no sign that it matters.

choices.text: No; the period of the pendulum did not change with string length in either experiment
choices.rationale: The period of the pendulum did change with string length; the point is that the condition made no difference.

choices.text: Yes; the period of the pendulum increased as string length increased in both experiments
choices.rationale: That trend concerns string length, not the mass of the bob, and appears identically in both experiments.

choices.text: Yes; the period of the pendulum was higher for 100 g bob than for 50 g bob at every string length
choices.rationale: The two columns are identical, so neither condition gave higher values.

explanation: Experiments 1 and 2 differ only in the mass of the bob, and every value is the same in both, so the results do not support the claim.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students hung a metal bob from a string using a 50 g bob, pulled the bob 10° to one side, and released it. They timed 10 complete swings with a stopwatch and divided by 10 to find the period. The procedure was repeated for several string lengths. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated using a 100 g bob, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: To decide whether the road surface has an effect on the tread depth, a student should compare the results of:

choices.text: Experiment 2 alone, because it was the only experiment performed on gravel roads
choices.rationale: Experiment 2 also used only one setting of the road surface; a comparison is required.

choices.text: Experiment 1 alone, because it tested the full range of the distance driven under one condition
choices.rationale: Experiment 1 used a single setting of the road surface, so by itself it cannot reveal its effect.

choices.text: Neither experiment, because the distance driven was varied in both of them
choices.rationale: Varying distance driven in both experiments is what makes them comparable row by row; the comparison across experiments is exactly what is needed.

choices.text: Experiments 1 and 2 together, because they differ only in the road surface
choices.rationale: Correct. Only by comparing results obtained under the two conditions, with everything else the same, can the effect of that condition be isolated.

explanation: Each experiment holds the road surface fixed at one setting; the two settings differ between experiments, so comparing Experiments 1 and 2 isolates its effect.

stimulus.title: Distance Driven and Tire Wear
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
A testing company fitted new tires of one model to the same car on paved roads and measured the tread depth with a gauge after each 10,000 km of driving on a fixed route.
Results (the tread depth): at 10000 km, 7.3 mm; at 20000 km, 6.4 mm; at 30000 km, 5.5 mm; at 40000 km, 4.6 mm; at 50000 km, 3.7 mm.

Experiment 2
The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated on gravel roads, with everything else unchanged.
Results: at 10000 km, 6.7 mm; at 20000 km, 5.2 mm; at 30000 km, 3.7 mm; at 40000 km, 2.2 mm; at 50000 km, 0.7 mm.

prompt: Suppose Experiment 1 were repeated with a temperature of 30°C, a setting between those used in Experiments 1 and 2. At pH 7, the activity of the enzyme would most likely be:

choices.text: between 75 µmol/min and 111 µmol/min
choices.rationale: Correct. At pH 7, Experiment 1 gave 75 and Experiment 2 gave 111; an intermediate setting should give an intermediate result.

choices.text: above both experiments' results, greater than 111 µmol/min
choices.rationale: This is above both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: below both experiments' results, less than 75 µmol/min
choices.rationale: This is below both experiments' results at this row; an intermediate setting should not fall outside them.

choices.text: between 42 µmol/min and 61 µmol/min
choices.rationale: These are the results for pH 8, not pH 7.

explanation: The two experiments bracket the new setting, so the result at pH 7 should lie between 75 and 111 µmol/min.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Students added 1 mL of enzyme solution to tubes containing a substrate solution buffered to a set pH and kept the tubes at 25°C. They measured how much product formed in 5 minutes to find the activity. Each pH was tested in triplicate. Experiment 2: The procedure was repeated and kept the tubes at 35°C, with everything else unchanged. Table 1 lists the results of both experiments.

prompt: Which of the following is the most serious flaw in the procedure of Experiment 1?

choices.text: Only a single value of the proofing temperature was tested, so no trend could possibly be identified
choices.rationale: The results list 6 different values of temperature.

choices.text: The proofing temperature was deliberately changed from trial to trial instead of being held constant throughout
choices.rationale: Changing the independent variable is the point of the experiment, not a flaw.

choices.text: The recipe for the dough changed between trials, confounding the effect of the proofing temperature
choices.rationale: Correct. A second factor that changes along with the independent variable confounds the results.

choices.text: The height of the dough was measured in every trial rather than only in the final trial of the series
choices.rationale: The dependent variable must be measured in every trial.

explanation: Good design changes only temperature. Because the recipe for the dough also changed, any difference in dough height could be due to either factor.

stimulus.title: Proofing Temperature and Dough Rise
stimulus.text:
Experiment 1
Students prepared identical batches of bread dough and placed each batch in a measuring cylinder in an oven set to a fixed temperature. After one hour they recorded the height of the dough. Because of limited equipment, the recipe for the dough was different for each trial.
Results (the height of the dough): at 20 °C, 6.1 cm; at 25 °C, 8.7 cm; at 30 °C, 11.3 cm; at 35 °C, 10.0 cm; at 40 °C, 6.9 cm; at 45 °C, 5.3 cm.

prompt: Based on Experiment 1 alone, which of the following statements goes beyond what the data can support?

choices.text: The pitch of the song was greater at 40 g than at 60 g.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The pitch of the song was greater at 10 g than at 60 g.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The pitch of the song was greater at 20 g than at 40 g.
choices.rationale: This statement is directly supported by the listed results.

choices.text: The pitch of the song would keep decreasing beyond 60 g.
choices.rationale: Correct. No trials were run beyond 60 g, so the results cannot show what happens there.

explanation: Three of the statements can be checked against the table and hold. "The pitch of the song would keep decreasing beyond 60 g." cannot: no trials were run beyond 60 g, so the results cannot show what happens there.

table.caption: Experiment 1: Researchers recorded the songs of male birds of six species and measured the average pitch of each species' song. Body mass was taken as the average for adult males of the species. Table 1 lists the results.
